headline: The Used Car Industry Is Booming. This N.J. Campus Is Setting the Price.

paragraphs.text: Car dealerships and Super Bowl ads are the most visible part of the auto industry. But arguably the real action is in places like this vast rectangular building near Trenton, N.J.
Hundreds of vehicles change hands on sale days at this auction center owned by Manheim, a division of Cox Automotive. It is among the largest of about 80 U.S. auction hubs Manheim operates.

The center has 17 lanes, each with its own entrance and exit. Manheim workers, many of them retirees earning a few extra bucks, drive vehicles slowly through garage-style doors, past auctioneers calling out prices from podiums, then out the other side. The din is overwhelming.

The site, in Bordentown, N.J., sells about 4,500 vehicles a week, part of a $730 billion market for used cars. Measured by the number of vehicles sold, the used car market is now more than double the size of the new car market. The vehicles might be trade-ins, coming off leases, older rental cars or repossessed from owners who fell behind on monthly loan payments.

Most Americans can’t afford new cars and have to buy used vehicles. In October, the average sale price for a new car was more than $51,000, according to Cox, a record. Automakers have discontinued many affordable models, like the Nissan Versa and the Ford Escape, because they were less profitable than big pickups and sport utility vehicles.
“You don’t see a lot of cars under $25,000,” said Lenny LaRocca, who leads the U.S. automotive industry practice at KPMG.
That has only made places like Manheim’s Bordentown hub more important. Auctions play a large role in setting prices for used cars, affecting the finances of millions of Americans.

Used car prices have been following the new car market higher. The average retail price of a three-year-old used car was $33,000 in October, up 2 percent from a year earlier. But there were big differences among categories.

Prices for electric vehicles and fuel-efficient compact cars rose more than 6 percent in October as buyers looked to save money on fuel. Prices for less efficient luxury cars, pickups and sport utility vehicles slipped, according to the Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index, a closely watched benchmark that is based on sales at Bordentown and other auction centers.

So far this year, wholesale prices for the least fuel-efficient cars have fallen 15 percent while prices for the most efficient vehicles have risen 10 percent. “Gas prices matter,” Jeremy Robb, chief economist at Cox Automotive, told several reporters during a tour of the center.
Sixteen of the 25 fastest-selling used cars are electric, according to separate data from iSeeCars, an online shopping site.

On a recent sunny day, car dealers, typically men dressed in jeans or sweatpants, roamed the auction lanes, stepping carefully to avoid the moving vehicles and indicating bids with a nod or a raised hand.
A blue Mercedes-Benz wagon with a badly dented right side went for $9,800. A 2023 Subaru Outback went for $14,800. A top-of-the-line BMW sport utility vehicle sold for almost $60,000.
“There she goes,” shouted an auctioneer, declaring the winning bid for the BMW by banging a length of rubber hose like a gavel. The vehicle disappeared through a door back into the sunlight.

Most of the bidding, about 70 percent, is done online. Before vehicles go on sale, they are driven through a brightly lit tunnel where 40 cameras capture detailed images that bidders can scrutinize. Manheim’s employees also inspect vehicles and flag problems.
“Unlike a new car, every used car is unique,” said Grace Huang, president of Cox Automotive’s Inventory Solutions group, who oversees the auction centers.
The New Jersey site has body and repair shops where vehicles can be spruced up. Manheim offers software to help sellers decide whether to make fixes or sell vehicles as they are.

Thousands of cars and trucks wait in parking lots that cover most of the 350-acre site. More than once, gangs of thieves have broken through the high fences, topped with barbed wire, and made off with valuable vehicles.

A growing percentage of cars at the lot were repossessed from owners who are struggling financially. Rising prices are forcing buyers to stretch their budgets, often to the breaking point. In October, 18 percent of car loans were subprime, meaning they were taken out by buyers with poor credit histories, according to Cox.

Signs point to a used car market that will continue to be lively. The average car on U.S. roads is 13 years old — older than they’ve ever been. Many people who have been putting off replacing their ride may not be able to wait much longer.
“Most vehicles are not made to last longer than 13 years,” Mr. Robb, the chief economist, said.

The used-car market is also becoming an important source of revenue for carmakers. They have discovered that they can make good money selling parts like floor mats or subscriptions to features like adaptive cruise control.
“A little known secret,” Mr. LaRocca of KPMG said, is that carmakers “actually make a lot of money in their aftermarket business.”
